title: Propositional Logic
html:
A knowledge-based agent stores facts as sentences in a formal language and derives new facts by inference. Propositional logic is the simplest such language: sentences are built from true/false symbols with connectives.

TELL the KB what is perceived
→
ASK the KB what to do (inference)
→
TELL the KB the action taken

Syntax and semantics

ConnectiveSymbolRead asTrue when
Negation¬Pnot PP is false
ConjunctionP ∧ QP and Qboth are true
DisjunctionP ∨ QP or Qat least one is true
ImplicationP ⇒ Qif P then QP is false or Q is true
BiconditionalP ⇔ QP if and only if Qboth have the same value
Watch out

P ⇒ Q is true whenever P is false (“if pigs fly, 1 = 2” is true). Implication in logic states no causal link — only that the case “P true, Q false” does not happen.

Key vocabulary

TermMeaning
ModelAn assignment of true/false to every symbol — a possible world
Entailment KB ⊨ αα is true in every model where the KB is true
Inference KB ⊢ αAn algorithm derives α from the KB
SoundDerives only entailed sentences (never lies)
CompleteCan derive every entailed sentence
Valid (tautology)True in all models: P ∨ ¬P
SatisfiableTrue in at least one model; unsatisfiable = true in none
Key point

Two facts power all of logical inference: KB ⊨ α iff KB ⇒ α is valid (deduction theorem), and iff KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable (proof by contradiction — the basis of resolution).

Inference by model checking

The simplest sound and complete method: enumerate every model (a truth table) and check that α holds wherever the KB holds. KB: If it rains the grass is wet (R ⇒ W), the sprinkler is on or it rains (S ∨ R), the sprinkler is off (¬S).

Model checking is exact but costs O(2ⁿ) for n symbols. Real systems use theorem proving (inference rules) or SAT solvers, which search the models cleverly.

Standard equivalences

NameEquivalence
Implication eliminationP ⇒ Q ≡ ¬P ∨ Q
ContrapositionP ⇒ Q ≡ ¬Q ⇒ ¬P
Biconditional eliminationP ⇔ Q ≡ (P ⇒ Q) ∧ (Q ⇒ P)
De Morgan¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q, ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q
Double negation¬¬P ≡ P
DistributivityP ∨ (Q ∧ R) ≡ (P ∨ Q) ∧ (P ∨ R)
Inference ruleFromInfer
Modus ponensP ⇒ Q, PQ
Modus tollensP ⇒ Q, ¬Q¬P
And-eliminationP ∧ QP
ResolutionP ∨ Q, ¬Q ∨ RP ∨ R
What is the difference between entailment and inference?

Entailment (⊨) is a semantic relationship: α is true in every model of the KB. Inference (⊢) is a syntactic procedure that derives sentences. A good inference procedure is sound (derives only entailed sentences) and complete (derives all of them).

How do you check whether KB entails α?

Either enumerate all models and check α in each model of the KB (truth tables, O(2ⁿ)), or show that KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable — with resolution or a SAT solver.
